posts.quote: MY THANKSGIVING PREP SO FAR IS KNOWING WHERE THE ROASTING PAN ISN'T.
posts.caption: I have a hosting plan, a guest list, and no idea where the roasting pan went. I checked the cabinet with a flashlight like it owed me money. It did not respond.
posts.first: Found a lid to something. Found a different lid to something else. The pan itself is apparently on an extended vacation, and I've decided to let it have one.
posts.alt: Comic-panel cartoon of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun kneeling in front of an open cabinet with pots and lids spilling out, holding a flashlight. Text at the top reads: My Thanksgiving prep so far is knowing where the roasting pan isn't.

posts.quote: I BAKED BANANA BREAD SO THE HOUSE WOULD SMELL LIKE I HAVE MY LIFE TOGETHER. THE BREAD HAS ITS LIFE TOGETHER. I'M JUST THE STAFF.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a plump woman with short mauve-pink curls and slippers sitting happily at a kitchen table beside a cooling loaf of banana bread and a glass of wine. Text at the top reads: I baked banana bread so the house would smell like I have my life together. The bread has its life together. I'm just the staff.

posts.quote: I BENT DOWN TO TIE MY SHOE AND SPENT A MOMENT DECIDING IF I'D COME BACK UP.
posts.caption: It was a quiet decision made halfway down. Everything works, technically, but nobody mentions that the return trip needs a plan. I tied the shoe and came back up in stages, dignity mostly intact.
posts.first: The other shoe stayed untied on purpose. One bend a day is my limit and I've already used it. I'm calling them slip-ons now.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun crouching in a hallway tying a sneaker with a thoughtful resigned expression. Text at the top reads: I bent down to tie my shoe and spent a moment deciding if I'd come back up.

posts.quote: WRINKLES I CAN HANDLE. IT'S THE TINY PRINT ON THE PILL BOTTLE AND A TOILET SEAT SITTING A FOOT TOO LOW THAT'S GOING TO TAKE ME OUT.
posts.caption: The pharmacy slipped a little magnifying card into my bag with the last refill. Nobody said anything. I keep it in the glove box now, next to the napkins and a flashlight I trust more than most people.
posts.first: I read the label under the lamp, then at arm's length, then out loud to the dog, who wasn't concerned. The dog is a fine editor.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun squinting at a small pill bottle held at arm's length in a pale blue bathroom with a low toilet behind her. Text at the top reads: Wrinkles I can handle. It's the tiny print on the pill bottle and a toilet seat sitting a foot too low that's going to take me out.

posts.quote: DAYLIGHT'S GETTING SHORTER, WHICH IS FINE. I WASN'T DOING SHIT WITH IT ANYWAY.
posts.caption: My days have always had a big middle where the sun was out and I was inside, and nothing has changed except the sun's schedule. I used to feel a little guilty about the unused hours. Now there are fewer of them, and the guilt is on a reduced shift. By four-thirty the lamp is on, the slippers are on, and the day has officially stopped asking things of me. I think this is what people mean by a good rhythm. I've been in it all along.
posts.first: I put the porch light on at 4:50 yesterday and felt oddly proud, like I'd closed a shop. The dog was in bed by 5:10. We keep the same hours, he and I, and neither of us has ever filed a complaint.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a plump woman with short mauve-pink curls reclining in a floral armchair by a window at dusk, feet up in fluffy slippers, holding a glass of wine beside a glowing lamp. Text at the top reads: Daylight's getting shorter, which is fine. I wasn't doing shit with it anyway.

posts.quote: Every pill I take comes with a list of side effects. It's longer than my list of reasons for taking it.
posts.alt: Plain off-white card with bold dark text that reads: Every pill I take comes with a list of side effects. It's longer than my list of reasons for taking it.

posts.quote: THE AUTOMATED VOICE SAID MY CALL WAS IMPORTANT. IT HAS BEEN SAYING THAT FOR FORTY MINUTES.
posts.caption: Forty minutes in, I know the hold music better than songs I actually like. The voice returns every few minutes to remind me I matter. I believe it a little less each time.
posts.first: I eventually got a person. She was lovely and fixed everything in ninety seconds, which made the forty minutes feel personal. I thanked her twice and hung up oddly emotional.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun sitting on a couch with a phone on speaker and a tired flat stare, a wall clock behind her. Text at the top reads: The automated voice said my call was important. It has been saying that for forty minutes.

posts.quote: THE STORES PUT UP CHRISTMAS DECORATIONS BEFORE THE HALLOWEEN CANDY WAS GONE. I BOUGHT BOTH AND I'M HOLDING THE STORE RESPONSIBLE.
posts.caption: There was a full eight-foot tree next to a bin of half-price candy, and a woman in a Halloween sweatshirt standing between them like a referee. I paused to admire the commitment of whoever planned the aisle. Then I took one ornament, one bag of candy, and a roll of wrapping paper I had no plans for. The cashier didn't blink. I've already spent more on holiday things than I meant to this month, and it's barely started. At least the candy won't last the week.
posts.first: The ornament is a small glass pickle. I don't know why. It's on the shelf by the front door now and it's the most cheerful thing in the house.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun standing in a store aisle holding a bag of candy and a red ornament beside a tall artificial Christmas tree and a bin of orange candy. Text at the top reads: The stores put up Christmas decorations before the Halloween candy was gone. I bought both and I'm holding the store responsible.

posts.quote: I FOUND THE REMOTE IN THE REFRIGERATOR NEXT TO THE BUTTER. I HAVE NO MEMORY OF THIS, AND I'M NOT ASKING THE BUTTER.
posts.caption: It still worked. That's what bothers me. I pressed the volume button standing in the open fridge, and the TV in the next room got louder. I closed the door and went to sit down.
posts.first: I put it back on the arm of the couch where it belongs and sat very still for a while. The couch looked at me. So did the dog. Nobody mentioned the refrigerator.
posts.alt: Comic-panel cartoon of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun holding a TV remote in front of an open refrigerator with butter and mustard on the shelf, looking baffled. Text at the top reads: I found the remote in the refrigerator next to the butter. I have no memory of this, and I'm not asking the butter.

posts.quote: I USED TO PLAN AHEAD. NOW I PLAN TO SIT DOWN.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a silver-haired woman in lavender-tinted round glasses and an oatmeal cardigan sitting barefoot in a sunroom armchair holding a mug. Text at the top reads: I used to plan ahead. Now I plan to sit down.

posts.quote: I GOT OUT THE GOOD DISHES TO CHECK THEM BEFORE THANKSGIVING. EIGHT PLATES SURVIVED. I'M ALREADY DECIDING WHO GETS THE EVERYDAY ONES.
posts.caption: The good dishes live on the top shelf of the dining room cabinet behind a tablecloth I received as a wedding gift and have used twice. Every year there is a ritual: take down the stack, wash each plate by hand, hold it to the light like a jeweler. This year there was a chip I'd forgotten, a crack I'd chosen not to remember, and a gravy stain from 2019 that is, at this point, part of the family. I washed everything anyway. The cabinet is quiet again. It knows.
posts.first: My mother had twelve of everything. I've never found out what happened to the other four when it came down to me. I suspect a church function. I'm still not ready to bring it up with the church.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun holding a white china plate up to the light beside a table stacked with plates and an open china cabinet. Text at the top reads: I got out the good dishes to check them before Thanksgiving. Eight plates survived. I'm already deciding who gets the everyday ones.

posts.quote: SCROLLING A WEBSITE'S DROPDOWN ALL THE WAY BACK TO MY BIRTH YEAR IS THE MOST HUMBLING SHIT I DO ALL DAY.
posts.caption: The year list starts at the current one and goes down like an elevator in a building I used to work in. I scroll past the nineties, the eighties, and a stretch of the seventies where I was apparently a child. Then I stop and pretend that's fine.
posts.first: I tried typing the year instead. It took me to 1993. I accepted this as fate, got my coupon, and left a slightly younger person than I came in.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun and glasses on her forehead sitting at a desk with a deadpan stare at a laptop showing a very long list of years. Text at the top reads: Scrolling a website's dropdown all the way back to my birth year is the most humbling shit I do all day.

posts.quote: THE COUCH HAS A DENT IN THE SHAPE OF MY BEST DECISIONS.
posts.caption: It took years of dedicated effort to get that shape right. Left cushion, slight angle, one arm on the pillow. It fits me exactly and has never once asked me to be anywhere.
posts.first: Visitors are offered the other end. They sit there politely while the dent waits. It remembers who it belongs to.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a plump woman with short mauve-pink curls lying contentedly on a floral sofa with a dent in the cushions, wearing fluffy slippers beside a wine glass. Text at the top reads: The couch has a dent in the shape of my best decisions.

posts.quote: I used to stay out until midnight. Now I'm in bed by nine, awake by two, and thinking about something I said in 1998.
posts.alt: Plain off-white card with bold dark text that reads: I used to stay out until midnight. Now I'm in bed by nine, awake by two, and thinking about something I said in 1998.

posts.quote: I ALREADY KNOW THE ANSWER. I JUST LIKE WATCHING YOU COMMIT TO THE LIE.
posts.caption: The cookies were on the counter at three. At four there were nine instead of twelve, and a very quiet dog with a crumb on his chin. I didn't say anything. I put the kettle on, took my time, and mentioned to the dog how his afternoon had been. He looked at the wall. He looked at the door. He looked at the plate, then away, as though it had never been introduced to him. It was the best performance I've seen since the community play in 2004. I let him have the last one.
posts.first: He's fourteen and has never once learned to hide the evidence. I think he wants to be caught. It's the only thing in the house that works that way.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun standing in a kitchen with crossed arms and a raised eyebrow, looking at a guilty dog with cookie crumbs on its chin. Text at the top reads: I already know the answer. I just like watching you commit to the lie.

posts.quote: I'M BRINGING THE ROLLS TO THANKSGIVING. THEY'RE FROM A BAKERY AND THEY'RE GOING IN MY OWN DISH. NOBODY NEEDS THE DETAILS.
posts.caption: I've been assigned rolls for six years, and for six years I've said I'll make them. The recipe is in my mother's handwriting, which I can read about two-thirds of. There's a word in the middle that is either scald or scold, and either one sounds like a threat. So on the morning of, I go to the bakery, buy two dozen, and warm them in the good casserole dish with a dish towel on top. They arrive looking homemade. I get complimented every year. I accept it.
posts.first: My aunt asked for the recipe once. I told her it was a family secret. It's the truest thing I've said at a holiday. I've since looked up scald, and I'm still not sure.
posts.alt: Comic-panel cartoon of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun tipping bakery rolls from a paper bag into a casserole dish with a sly sideways glance. Text at the top reads: I'm bringing the rolls to Thanksgiving. They're from a bakery and they're going in my own dish. Nobody needs the details.

stories.quote: THE THANKSGIVING RECIPE SAYS SERVES EIGHT. I'M SERVING FOUR AND KEEPING THE REST AS A REWARD.
stories.alt: Comic-panel cartoon of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun resting her chin on her hand at a kitchen table with an open cookbook showing a roast turkey and a glass of red wine, autumn leaves outside. Text at the top reads: The Thanksgiving recipe says serves eight. I'm serving four and keeping the rest as a reward.

stories.quote: I GOT INTO A STARING CONTEST WITH THE THERMOSTAT. IT SAID 68. MY BODY SAID OTHERWISE. NOBODY BLINKED.
stories.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun standing in a hallway with arms crossed and a wine glass, giving a sideways glare at a wall thermostat reading 68 while a cat looks up at her. Text in the speech bubble reads: I got into a staring contest with the thermostat. It said 68. My body said otherwise. Nobody blinked.

stories.quote: I STOOD UP TOO FAST AND THE ROOM ASKED ME TO RECONSIDER.
stories.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun gripping a kitchen chair with wide dizzy eyes and little stars around her head, holding a glass of wine. Text at the top reads: I stood up too fast and the room asked me to reconsider.

stories.quote: I DON'T MISS GOING OUT. I MISS GOING OUT AND BEING HOME BY SEVEN.
stories.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with short mauve-pink curls relaxing in a floral armchair in fluffy slippers with a mug and a plaid blanket, a coat on a hook and a wall clock showing seven, a cat asleep at her feet. Text at the top reads: I don't miss going out. I miss going out and being home by seven.
